interactions.label: A woman delivered vaginally 3 hours ago. Her pulse is 120/min and systolic blood

params.question: A woman delivered vaginally 3 hours ago. Her pulse is 120/min and systolic blood pressure is 80 mmHg, giving a shock index of 1.5. Based on the thresholds discussed, this value most likely indicates:

answers.text: Normal postpartum physiology requiring observation only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A normal shock index is below 0.7–0.9. A value of 1.5 is markedly elevated and indicates significant haemodynamic compromise requiring urgent action.

answers.text: Compensated blood loss — oral uterotonics and monitoring are sufficient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Young, healthy women can appear deceptively stable due to compensatory mechanisms, but a shock index above 1.0 indicates true haemodynamic compromise. Waiting for overt hypotension risks dangerous delay.

answers.text: Haemodynamic compromise needing urgent transfusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A shock index above 1.0 signals haemodynamic compromise requiring urgent transfusion. This patient's value of 1.5 clearly exceeds that threshold but is below 1.7, which would indicate life-threatening haemorrhage.

answers.text: Life-threatening haemorrhage requiring massive transfusion protocol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Life-threatening haemorrhage is indicated by a shock index above 1.7. This patient's value of 1.5 indicates serious compromise needing urgent transfusion, but has not yet reached the life-threatening threshold.

overallFeedback.feedback: The shock index is calculated as heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. Values above 1.0 indicate haemodynamic compromise needing urgent transfusion; above 1.7 indicates life-threatening haemorrhage. Young women may compensate well, so don't wait for overt hypotension.
Well done. The shock index (heart rate ÷ systolic BP) is a rapid bedside tool: >1.0 signals compromise needing urgent transfusion, and >1.7 signals life-threatening haemorrhage.

interactions.label: Active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL) is recommended for every

params.question: Active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL) is recommended for every woman delivering, not just those identified as high risk. Which of the following best explains this practice?

answers.text: Risk factor screening reliably identifies most women who will develop PPH

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is actually the opposite of reality. Risk factor screening has poor predictive value — many women who develop PPH have no identifiable risk factors at all.

answers.text: Up to 40% of PPH cases occur in women with no identifiable risk factor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Because risk factor identification misses a large proportion of PPH cases, relying on selective prevention would leave many women unprotected. Universal AMTSL closes this gap.

answers.text: AMTSL is only effective when given to women without prior uterotonic exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: AMTSL is effective regardless of prior uterotonic exposure. Its universality is driven by the unpredictability of PPH, not by pharmacological limitations.

answers.text: Controlled cord traction can only be safely performed if initiated before the third stage begins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Controlled cord traction is one component of AMTSL performed during the third stage itself. The reason for universal AMTSL is the inability to predict which women will bleed, not a procedural timing constraint.

overallFeedback.feedback: Risk factor screening has limited predictive value: up to 40% of PPH cases occur in women with no identifiable risk factors. This is precisely why AMTSL is recommended universally rather than selectively.
Exactly. The unpredictability of PPH — with up to 40% of cases occurring in women without risk factors — is the key reason AMTSL is offered to all women, not selectively.

interactions.label: During management of atonic PPH unresponsive to uterotonics, a Bakri balloon is

params.question: During management of atonic PPH unresponsive to uterotonics, a Bakri balloon is inflated with 400 mL of warm saline inside the uterine cavity. Vaginal bleeding stops completely. What does this finding indicate?

answers.text: The uterus has regained its own tone and the balloon can be removed immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cessation of bleeding with the balloon in situ means the balloon is providing the tamponade, not the uterus. Removing it immediately risks re-bleeding. The balloon is typically left in place for 24–48 hours.

answers.text: A positive tamponade test — surgical intervention is unlikely to be needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When bleeding stops after balloon inflation, this is called a positive tamponade test. It indicates that mechanical tamponade alone is sufficient and surgical escalation — B-Lynch suture, devascularisation, or hysterectomy — is unlikely to be required.

answers.text: Retained placental fragments have been displaced and the bleeding source is sealed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The balloon works by exerting direct pressure against the uterine walls, compressing the placental bed vessels. It does not displace tissue fragments — the mechanism is tamponade, not tissue displacement.

answers.text: The balloon has triggered a sustained uterine contraction reflex

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the balloon may stimulate some uterine activity, the clinical significance of the tamponade test is that mechanical pressure alone is controlling the bleeding. The test predicts that surgical escalation is unlikely to be needed.

overallFeedback.feedback: When an intrauterine balloon is inflated and vaginal bleeding stops, this is called a positive tamponade test. It indicates that mechanical tamponade is sufficient to control bleeding, and surgical escalation is unlikely to be needed.
Correct. A positive tamponade test — bleeding stopping after balloon inflation — is a key decision point in the PPH escalation ladder, indicating that surgery is unlikely to be needed.

interactions.label: In acute uterine inversion, the cardiovascular collapse is often far more severe

params.question: In acute uterine inversion, the cardiovascular collapse is often far more severe than the volume of blood lost would explain. Which additional mechanism contributes to this disproportionate shock?

answers.text: Anaphylaxis from exposure of foetal antigens to the maternal circulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Foetal antigen exposure can cause amniotic fluid embolism, which is a separate and distinct condition. The disproportionate shock in uterine inversion is caused by a different mechanism related to mechanical displacement of the uterus.

answers.text: Vasovagal response triggered by traction on uterine ligaments and peritoneum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The inverted uterus pulls on its broad and round ligaments and the overlying peritoneum, triggering a parasympathetic (vasovagal) reflex that causes bradycardia and hypotension — on top of any haemorrhagic shock.

answers.text: Acute adrenal insufficiency from sudden loss of placental cortisol production

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Placental cortisol production ceases with delivery in all women, not specifically in uterine inversion. The disproportionate shock here is caused by a vasovagal reflex from peritoneal and ligament traction.

answers.text: Air embolism entering through the exposed placental sinuses on the inverted fundus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Air embolism is not a recognised mechanism in uterine inversion. The disproportionate shock is explained by the vasovagal reflex triggered by traction on the uterine ligaments and peritoneum.

overallFeedback.feedback: In acute uterine inversion, the inverted fundus tugs on the broad and round ligaments and peritoneum, triggering a parasympathetic (vasovagal) reflex with bradycardia and hypotension. This adds to haemorrhagic shock, explaining why collapse seems out of proportion to visible bleeding.

Well done. The vasovagal component — triggered by peritoneal and ligament traction — is what makes the shock in uterine inversion disproportionate to the blood loss, distinguishing this emergency from ordinary PPH.

interactions.label: A woman with acute uterine inversion has the placenta still attached to the inve

params.question: A woman with acute uterine inversion has the placenta still attached to the inverted fundus. Intravenous access has been secured and resuscitation is underway. What is the correct action regarding the placenta before attempting the Johnson manoeuvre?

answers.text: Remove the placenta to reduce the bulk of tissue that must be pushed back through the cervix

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Removing the placenta before reduction opens the placental sinuses on the inverted fundus, causing massive haemorrhage that cannot be controlled until the uterus is repositioned. The placenta must stay in place.

answers.text: Partially separate the placenta at its edges to allow a better grip on the fundus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Any degree of placental separation opens vascular sinuses on the exposed fundal surface. Even partial removal can trigger uncontrollable haemorrhage. Leave the placenta entirely undisturbed.

answers.text: Leave the placenta in place — it tamponades the placental bed and limits haemorrhage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The attached placenta covers and compresses the placental bed sinuses, limiting bleeding. Removing it before the uterus is reduced is the single most dangerous error in managing uterine inversion.

answers.text: Administer oxytocin to contract the uterus and separate the placenta before reduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oxytocin causes uterine contraction, which would tighten the cervical constriction ring around the inverted fundus and make reduction harder or impossible. Oxytocin is given only after successful reduction, never before.

overallFeedback.feedback: The attached placenta acts as a tamponade over the placental bed sinuses. Removing it before reduction opens those sinuses and triggers massive, uncontrollable haemorrhage. Leave the placenta in place, perform the Johnson manoeuvre, and only then manage the placenta and give oxytocin.

Exactly right. The placenta tamponades the placental bed and must be left undisturbed until the uterus has been successfully reduced by the Johnson manoeuvre. This is the single most critical rule in managing uterine inversion.
